passage: Last Wednesday I only went to Room 12 to collect the hall key, but I stayed to watch the annual-day committee. Arnab wrote the numbers 1 to 30 on the board and said, "No comments until we reach thirty." Ideas flew: a retro night, a monsoon carnival, an upside-down day. Someone said, "That's silly." Arnab just tapped the board and said, "Thirty first." When the board was full, they talked. Some ideas merged. Hands went up for the vote, and three were left: retro night, carnival, school in space. A boy near the window, who I'd never heard speak at a meeting, offered the last one, and it made the final three. I can't say what he felt, but he was smiling. - Kiran

qa.q: How many ideas did the committee list before discussing?
qa.a: The committee listed thirty ideas before discussing.

qa.q: What does Arnab's calm tapping of the board suggest, and how sure can Kiran be?
qa.a: Arnab seems calm and determined to keep ideas flowing without judgement, though Kiran can only guess from what was seen.

qa.q: What could the committee do next if all three finalists turn out too costly, and why?
qa.a: They could check cost and space for each and merge parts of the ideas, because everyone has already contributed and a workable choice can still be shaped.

qa.q: What was it like for the boy near the window when his idea was not judged?
qa.a: The boy probably felt safe enough to speak and proud when his idea reached the final three, since the rule stopped anyone from dismissing it. 😊

grounding: The committee lists thirty theme ideas without judging, then narrows to three by discussion and votes, so everyone contributes before converging on a workable choice.

passage:
Monday. Chaitanya taped chart paper to the classroom wall. "Farewell theme. Every idea goes up, even silly ones. Nobody says 'that won't work' until Wednesday." Farhan snorted but wrote "Space Station". By the last bell the sheet held thirty ideas, from "Old Film Posters" to "Board Games Night".

Wednesday. The committee circled back. "If we argue about thirty, we'll fight till March," Chaitanya said aloud. "Let's keep only what fits the hall and our budget." Talk trimmed the list to three: Retro Radio, Monsoon Fair, and Space Station. Twelve hands voted on slips folded into a lunchbox.

Friday. Monsoon Fair won by two votes. Farhan, whose idea lost, shrugged and offered to paint paper boats. "At least I got my rocket on the wall first," he said, grinning.

qa.q: How many ideas were on the chart paper by the last bell on Monday?
qa.a: By the last bell on Monday the sheet held thirty ideas.

qa.q: How does Farhan seem to feel when his Space Station idea loses the vote?
qa.a: Farhan seems good-humoured rather than hurt; he shrugs, grins and offers to paint paper boats, which suggests he feels his idea was heard and is content to help.

qa.q: What else could the committee have tried if the vote had ended in a tie?
qa.a: They could have asked each supporter to explain one practical benefit and then voted again, or merged two themes, so the choice still rests on reasons.

qa.q: How might a quiet committee member see this way of planning?
qa.a: A quiet member might feel included, because on Monday every idea went up without being judged, so they could add one without fear of being laughed at.

grounding: Shows a committee listing many theme ideas without judging, then narrowing to three by discussion and voting before choosing.

passage:
Sit, Vijay, you're making the chai go cold. You asked how your Asif chacha ever organised anything. Well, I was fifteen, and our school wanted a Founders' Day stall. Six of us, and everyone had a favourite idea and a loud voice. First meeting was pure shouting.

Our science teacher stopped us. "For twenty minutes, nobody may say no," she said. We filled the blackboard: a puppet show, a pickle sale, a quiz, a mehendi corner, even a snake charmer, which was mine. Then we talked, rubbed out what cost too much, and kept three. We voted with pebbles in a steel tumbler.

The quiz won. My snake charmer lost badly, and I sulked for an hour. But I ran the scoreboard, and nobody could say they hadn't been heard.

qa.q: What did the students use to vote?
qa.a: They voted with pebbles in a steel tumbler.

qa.q: How did young Asif feel when his snake charmer idea lost?
qa.a: He felt sulky and disappointed for about an hour, but that eased enough that he still ran the scoreboard.

qa.q: What turning point in the story changed the first shouting meeting?
qa.a: The teacher's rule that nobody could say no for twenty minutes turned shouting into listing; without it, the loudest voices would probably have picked the stall.

qa.q: How might the student whose quiz idea won have felt about the process?
qa.a: That student might feel proud, and also confident the choice was fair, because the quiz beat the other ideas in an open vote rather than by shouting.

grounding: An elder recalls a school stall where ideas were listed freely for a set time, cut down by discussion and chosen by vote.
